title: Can the numbers 1 to 17 make a row of square sums?
description: The numbers one to seventeen are placed in a row so that every neighbouring pair adds to a square. Keeko doubts where sixteen can sit, because a middle place seems fine.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number with only one possible partner must sit at an end of the row. Watch for students who start from one and try the numbers in order until they get stuck.

source: Arrange 1 to 17 in a row so that each pair of neighbours adds to a perfect square.
video_script.why: The child finds the numbers with only one possible partner, puts them at the two ends, and builds the row one forced neighbour at a time.
video_script.substitution: Find the numbers with one partner, put them at the ends, then add one forced neighbour at a time and check every sum.
video_script.anchor: number cards one to seventeen waiting to be put in a row
video_script.wrong_answer: sixteen can sit in the middle
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko puts sixteen in the middle of the row. In the middle a number needs two partners, but sixteen has only one, nine, so it must sit at an end.
video_script.payoff_line: Sixteen, nine, seven, two, fourteen, eleven, five, four, twelve, thirteen, three, six, ten, fifteen, one, eight, seventeen

final_answer.spoken: sixteen, nine, seven, two, fourteen, eleven, five, four, twelve, thirteen, three, six, ten, fifteen, one, eight, seventeen

maths_rules: the biggest possible sum is 17 + 16 = 33, so the possible square sums are 4, 9, 16 and 25
16 + 9 = 25 is the only way for 16, and 17 + 8 = 25 is the only way for 17, so 16 and 17 are the two ends
at 3 the choice is 6 or 1; choosing 1 gets stuck, choosing 6 forces 10, 15, 1, 8, 17
video_script.design: One idea: a number with one partner sits at an end, and the rest of the row is forced. Wrong idea: sixteen can sit in the middle. The number cards stay in the anchor band and the row builds on the working board.

narration: <bookmark mark='sums'/>Step one, list the possible squares. The biggest sum is seventeen plus sixteen, which is thirty three.
The squares that fit are four, nine, sixteen and twenty five.
<bookmark mark='sixteen'/>Sixteen needs a partner that makes twenty five. Only nine does that.
<bookmark mark='seventeen'/>Seventeen also has one partner, which is eight.
<bookmark mark='ends'/>A number with one partner can only sit at an end. Sixteen and seventeen are the two ends.

narration: <bookmark mark='nine'/>Step two, build the row from the sixteen end. Nine comes next.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>Nine needs a partner that makes sixteen, so seven comes next.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Seven needs two to make nine.
<bookmark mark='fourteen'/>Two needs fourteen to make sixteen.
<bookmark mark='go'/>Going on in the same way, each number is forced. The row grows by eleven, five, four, twelve, thirteen and three.

narration: <bookmark mark='choice'/>Step three, at three there is a choice, six or one.
<bookmark mark='stuck'/>Taking one first gets stuck, so we choose six.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Six needs ten, ten needs fifteen, fifteen needs one, one needs eight, and eight needs seventeen.
<bookmark mark='end'/>The row ends at seventeen, as it should.

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, put the answer back in the question and add each neighbouring pair.
<bookmark mark='sums'/>Sixteen plus nine is twenty five, and eight plus seventeen is twenty five too.
Every sum in between is sixteen or nine.
<bookmark mark='squares'/>Twenty five, sixteen and nine are all squares.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Here is the row.
